title: About Srivathsan
summary: Beyond code: hobbies, languages, what Srivathsan is learning right now, and where he's headed.
html:
Hobbies & interests

title: BCO Lead Automation
summary: An n8n + Apify pipeline that scrapes Ottawa tech-company directories and Google Maps into a scored lead list for Builders Collective Ottawa sponsorship outreach.
html:
Overview

A lead-generation automation pipeline built for Builders Collective Ottawa (BCO), a community/sponsorship-driven org, to build a scored list of Ottawa-area tech companies worth approaching for sponsorship. It's not a web app. It's a self-hosted n8n instance orchestrating scraper actors that feed a shared Google Sheet.

Problem

Finding and qualifying sponsorship-worthy tech companies in Ottawa by hand (checking member directories, searching maps by category, cross-referencing who's already been contacted) doesn't scale past a handful of leads at a time. The goal was an automated first pass that builds a deduplicated, scored candidate list, leaving the human judgment (relevance, sponsorship capacity, personalized outreach) for after the raw list exists.

What I built

  • A self-hosted n8n instance (Docker Compose, forked from a local n8n template) running two workflows on manual triggers
  • Directory scraper workflow: pulls the Kanata North Business Association member directory, Invest Ottawa's company list, and the Ottawa Board of Trade tech directory via Apify actors, normalizes results, and appends them to a Raw - Directories sheet
  • Google Maps scraper workflow: runs 6 category searches (software, AI, cybersecurity, cloud, telecom, robotics) via an Apify Google Maps actor, capped at 20 results each (~120 max) with contact enrichment/reviews/images deliberately disabled to control Apify's per-result cost, appending to Raw - Google Maps
  • Both workflows dedupe and upsert into a shared Master Leads sheet using a Dedup Key, with manual scoring columns (BCO Relevance, Sponsorship Capacity, Ottawa Presence, Community Signal → Priority Score) for a human to fill in afterward
  • A GCP project holding the service account/OAuth credentials and IAM permissions that let n8n read and write the shared Google Sheet
  • BCO Leads 2.0: an enrichment pass built with Claude Code on top of the raw V1 scrape, adding per-company contact emails, personalization hooks, and outreach-status tracking, covering the KNBA and Invest Ottawa lead sets
  • The V1 n8n workflows themselves were built with Claude and Cursor as AI pair-programmers for the workflow/config authoring

Architecture

n8n (Docker Compose, port 5678, persistent n8n_data volume) is the orchestration layer. Each workflow calls out to Apify actors via HTTP request nodes, one hitting a general web-scraper actor against directory pages, the other hitting a Google Maps scraper actor, using APIFY_TOKEN. Results are normalized in n8n, filtered (directory results by tech keywords; maps results by category), and written to Google Sheets (BCO_GOOGLE_SHEET_ID) via upsert nodes keyed on a computed dedup key. Access to that sheet is governed by a GCP project (service account credentials and IAM permissions scoped to the Sheets API) rather than a personal Google account, so read/write access to Master Leads can be managed and revoked independently of any one person's login. Both workflows are manually triggered, not scheduled. This is a run-on-demand pipeline, not a fully autonomous one.

Currently two disconnected halves: the checked-in SETUP_README.md is explicit that this V1 pipeline does not find individual employees, enrich contact details, draft emails, or send outreach. A separate folder in the repo (Recovered KNBA and Invest Ottawa files/) does contain exactly that (contact emails, personalization hooks, outreach status per company), produced by BCO Leads 2.0, a Claude Code-driven enrichment pass run independently of the n8n workflows. The scraping automation (V1) and the enrichment work (2.0) aren't wired together into one pipeline yet.

Decisions

  • n8n + Apify over a custom scraper: let the pipeline reuse battle-tested scraper actors (web + Google Maps) instead of writing and maintaining scraping/anti-bot logic from scratch, at the cost of Apify's per-run pricing.
  • Manual triggers over a schedule: kept the pipeline run-on-demand while still validating the approach, rather than scheduling runs before knowing the data was actually useful.
  • Capping Google Maps results and disabling enrichment per search: a deliberate cost control: 20 results × 6 categories keeps the Apify bill predictable while still giving broad category coverage.

Results

A working, repeatable pipeline that produces a deduplicated Master Leads sheet from two independent sources (member directories + Google Maps), ready for manual scoring, plus a BCO Leads 2.0 enrichment pass that added contact emails, personalization hooks and outreach tracking for the KNBA and Invest Ottawa leads.

What I learned

  • Splitting "find candidates" from "qualify and personalize" into separate stages made it possible to ship the scraping half without having solved contact enrichment yet.
  • Deliberately disabling expensive Apify enrichment options up front (reviews, images, contact details) kept early iteration cheap while the workflow shape was still changing.
  • A stable dedup key is what makes multi-source scraping usable. The same company can appear in several directories and on Google Maps, and upserting on one computed key keeps Master Leads to one row per company.
  • Give automations their own credentials. A GCP service account for Sheets access means the pipeline doesn't depend on, or break with, anyone's personal Google login.
  • AI pair-programming (Claude, Cursor, Claude Code) sped up both the n8n workflow authoring and the enrichment pass, but leaving the two halves unconnected showed that stages built separately need a plan for how they join.

What's next

  • Connect BCO Leads 2.0's Claude Code enrichment pass back into the automated V1 pipeline so scraping and enrichment run as one flow
  • Consider moving from manual triggers to a schedule once the workflow shape is settled

title: Brain Tumor Detection Model
summary: A CNN that classifies glioma vs. healthy brain MRI slices, with Grad-CAM heatmaps so the prediction is explainable, not just a label.
html:
Overview

A deep learning pipeline that classifies MRI slices as glioma vs. healthy, trained on the UCSF-PDGM collection from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA). The project isn't just a classifier: it also produces Grad-CAM heatmaps so a prediction comes with a visual explanation of which region of the brain drove it, rather than a bare label.

Problem

Tumor screening from MRI is slow and reviewer-dependent, and a black-box classifier that just outputs "glioma" or "healthy" isn't trustworthy enough to reason about. There's no way to check why the model thinks what it thinks. The goal was a model that's both accurate and inspectable.

What I built

  • A CNN image classifier trained on central MRI slices extracted from DICOM/NIfTI volumes (data_prep.py, make_dataset.py)
  • A training pipeline with data augmentation for robustness and automatic best-checkpoint saving (train.py, model.py)
  • An evaluation pass reporting precision, recall, F1, and a precision-recall curve (evaluate.py)
  • Grad-CAM heatmap generation to visualize which brain regions influenced each prediction (grad_cam.py)

Architecture

Raw MRI volumes (DICOM/NIfTI) go through data_prep.py, which extracts central slices and converts them into NumPy arrays (X.npy/y.npy). train.py loads those arrays, does a stratified 70/15/15 train/val/test split, and fits a CNN:

  • 3 conv blocks (32 → 64 → 128 filters, 3×3, ReLU, same padding) each followed by 2×2 max-pooling, over a single-channel 224×224 input
  • Flatten → Dense(128, ReLU) → Dropout(0.5) → Dense(1, sigmoid) for binary glioma-vs-healthy output
  • Adam optimizer (lr 1e-4), binary crossentropy, trained up to 40 epochs with EarlyStopping (patience 5 on val_loss) and ModelCheckpoint saving the best weights to models/best_model.h5
  • Light augmentation on the training set only: ±10° rotation, 5% width/height shift, 10% zoom, horizontal flip; batch size 16

evaluate.py and grad_cam.py both load a saved checkpoint. One scores it against the held-out test split, and the other renders heatmaps for individual predictions.

Decisions

  • Central-slice extraction over full 3D volumes: trades some spatial context for a much smaller, faster-to-train 2D CNN (single-channel 224×224 input) than a volumetric model would need, which mattered more for a first working version than squeezing out volumetric accuracy.
  • A deliberately simple 3-block CNN over a pretrained backbone: kept the model small and fast to iterate on for a first version, at the cost of whatever accuracy a transfer-learned backbone might have added.
  • Grad-CAM instead of a plain classifier: treats interpretability as a first-class requirement rather than an afterthought, since a medical-imaging prediction without a "why" is hard to trust or debug.

Results

A complete pipeline from raw MRI volumes to a trained classifier: evaluation reports precision, recall, F1-score and a precision-recall curve on the held-out 15% test split, and Grad-CAM renders a heatmap for any individual prediction.

What I learned

  • Interpretability tooling (Grad-CAM) is worth building alongside the model, not bolted on after. It changed how I debugged misclassifications during training.
  • Medical imaging formats (DICOM/NIfTI) need real preprocessing discipline before they're usable as flat training arrays: reading two volume formats, picking the central slice and producing consistent single-channel 224×224 inputs all happen before the model sees anything.
  • Start simple, then scale. A 3-block CNN on central 2D slices got a working end-to-end pipeline quickly, and it gives a baseline that 3D or pretrained models have to beat.
  • Precision and recall say more than accuracy in medical screening, where a missed tumor and a false alarm have very different costs.
  • A stratified split keeps the glioma-to-healthy ratio the same across train, validation and test, so the test metrics reflect the real class balance.

What's next

  • Multi-modal MRI input (T1, T1-CE, T2, FLAIR) instead of a single sequence
  • 3D CNN models trained on full MRI volumes instead of central slices
  • Clinical label prediction (e.g. IDH mutation status)

title: CRA Audit Knowledge Retrieval
summary: The retrieval foundation (semantic + keyword + graph) for a planned future RAG system over a hand-curated vault of CRA audit-methodology notes. Not yet shipped; generation is still to come.
html:
Overview

A work-in-progress project to build a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) system over a hand-curated knowledge base of Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) audit methodology: organization structure, audit-methodology practices, statistics, software-controls, risk-control frameworks, and 6 public audit/evaluation case studies, sourced from official canada.ca documentation rather than any forum or community content. Current state: retrieval foundation only, not shipped: the hybrid retrieval layer (semantic + keyword + graph) is built and evaluated, but the generation step that would make this a complete RAG system hasn't been built yet; today a query returns ranked, explained source notes, not a synthesized answer. It's also worth being upfront that the retrieval code (rag/, eval/) is currently local-only and not yet pushed to the public GitHub repo, which today only reflects the earlier vault-content commits.

Problem

Public CRA audit documentation is comprehensive but scattered across many separate official pages and methodology documents, so finding the right source note for a specific audit question means either already knowing where to look or manually searching each source. The goal was a retrieval layer that could surface the most relevant, properly-sourced notes for a question, with a transparent explanation of why each result was ranked where it was. A black-box answer wouldn't work, since audit findings need to be traceable to their source.

What I built

  • A hand-curated Obsidian vault of ~444 markdown notes (~289 substantive, ~155 infrastructure/index notes) organized into numbered folders (00-Start through 99-Sources), each source note carrying YAML frontmatter with source_url, publisher, and accessed_on pointing back to the originating canada.ca page
  • corpus.py / chunking.py: walk the vault and split notes into retrieval-sized chunks
  • embeddings.py: embed chunks locally with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (no API key or per-call cost) into a flat NumPy array used directly as the vector store, with no external vector DB service
  • lexical.py: a parallel BM25 keyword index (rank-bm25) for exact-term matching semantic search can miss
  • graph.py: a networkx graph built from the vault's own note-to-note wikilinks (Obsidian-style double-bracket links between notes), used for n-hop graph-proximity expansion
  • retrieve.py: blends semantic similarity, BM25 score, graph proximity, and an authoritative-source bonus into one weighted hybrid score, with a why_included explanation attached to every result
  • A CLI (python -m rag.cli {index|search|stats}) as the only interface (no web UI or chat interface yet)
  • A real evaluation harness (eval/retrieval_eval.py, eval/questions.json, 10 hand-written Q&A pairs with expected notes) computing Hit@1/3/5, Recall@5/10, and MRR across multiple retrieval modes

Architecture

Vault markdown (vault/public/...-style folder structure, curated by hand) → corpus.py/chunking.py build chunked documents → embeddings.py produces a local NumPy embedding matrix (rag_data/embeddings.npy) while lexical.py builds a BM25 index (rag_data/lexical_bm25.pkl) and graph.py builds a wikilink graph (rag_data/graph.json) in parallel. retrieve.py queries all three signals plus a source-authority bonus and combines them into a single ranked, explained result list, exposed only via the CLI. No LLM is called anywhere in the pipeline.

Decisions

  • Local embeddings over an API-based embedding model: sentence-transformers running locally means no per-query cost and no external dependency, at the cost of lower embedding quality than a larger hosted model.
  • A flat NumPy array over a dedicated vector database: reasonable at the current corpus size (~289 substantive notes); would need revisiting if the corpus grew by an order of magnitude.
  • Hybrid retrieval (semantic + BM25 + graph) over semantic search alone: combines what embeddings are good at (conceptual similarity) with what BM25 is good at (exact term matches embeddings can miss) and what the graph adds (notes the author explicitly linked as related), rather than betting on one signal.
  • Building and proving out retrieval before generation: the plan is a full RAG system, but getting hybrid retrieval right first (and evaluating it) means the eventual generation step will be grounded in results already shown to be accurate, rather than layering an LLM on top of unproven retrieval over audit-sensitive content.

Results

On the 10-question hand-written eval set, the hybrid_graph retrieval mode reaches Hit@1 = 0.9 and MRR = 0.91. That's strong on this small set, but 10 questions is not a statistically robust benchmark and shouldn't be read as a general accuracy number.

What I learned

  • Building the eval harness alongside the retrieval pipeline (rather than after) made it possible to compare hybrid and single-signal retrieval modes with real numbers instead of eyeballing results.
  • Each retrieval signal covers a different weakness. Embeddings find conceptually similar notes but blur exact terms; BM25 catches exact terms like program names and acronyms; the wikilink graph brings in notes I had explicitly linked as related. Blending them is more robust than betting on any one.
  • Curation is half the work in a RAG system. Sourcing every note from official canada.ca pages, with source_url, publisher and accessed_on in its frontmatter, is what makes each result traceable and its why_included explanation meaningful.
  • A small eval set is still worth having. Ten hand-written questions were enough to compare modes and catch regressions, as long as the numbers aren't presented as a general accuracy figure.
  • Proving retrieval before adding generation keeps problems separable: if a future answer is wrong, I can check whether retrieval surfaced the right notes before blaming the LLM.

What's next

  • Build the generation layer on top of this retrieval foundation to complete the planned RAG implementation: an LLM that answers a question using the retrieved, source-traceable notes as grounding
  • Commit the rag/ and eval/ retrieval code so the public repo reflects the actual current state of the project
  • Grow the eval question set beyond 10 questions for a more robust accuracy signal

title: Eco Intelligence Dashboard
summary: A Next.js admin dashboard, based on the open-source TailAdmin template, built for TechnataHack24 to monitor router activity, energy savings, and heat management.
html:
Overview

The frontend of Eco Intelligence, built for the TechnataHack24 hackathon: a dashboard meant to give IT administrators a real-time view of router activity, energy savings, and heat/thermal management. I built it on the open-source TailAdmin Next.js admin template so the team had a polished, chart-ready admin shell from the first hour. The committed repo is that shell, rebranded as the Eco-Intelligence user dashboard: layout, navigation, chart components and animation are in place, while the router-, energy- and heat-specific widgets and the backend connection described in the README were the layer planned on top of it and aren't in the committed code.

Problem

IT infrastructure teams don't have a simple, live view of how much energy their network hardware is actually consuming, or when equipment is running hot, so energy waste and overheating both go unnoticed until they're expensive.

What I built

  • A Next.js admin dashboard scaffolded from the TailAdmin template and rebranded as the Eco-Intelligence user dashboard, as the base for an IT energy/heat monitoring tool
  • Chart-driven views (ApexCharts) ready for presenting router and energy time-series data
  • An animated, responsive UI via Framer Motion

Architecture

Next.js (App Router) frontend styled with Tailwind CSS, charting via react-apexcharts, and transitions via Framer Motion. The plan was a REST connection to a separate backend serving router status and energy/heat predictions; that integration isn't part of this repo, so the dashboard renders the template's sample data.

Decisions

  • TailAdmin as a starting scaffold over a from-scratch dashboard: got a polished, chart-ready admin UI in place immediately under hackathon time pressure, rather than spending hackathon hours on dashboard-shell plumbing.

Results

Submitted to TechnataHack24 as the dashboard frontend for the Eco Intelligence concept.

What I learned

  • A template buys time under hackathon pressure only if the saved time goes into the domain-specific views. The shell came together fast; the router, energy and heat widgets that would have made it Eco Intelligence are the part that didn't make it in.
  • Agree on the data contract with the backend early. Without a defined API to code against, the frontend had nothing real to chart and stayed on sample data.
  • Keep the README honest to the code. It describes GSAP animations and a live backend connection the committed code doesn't have (the animation library is actually Framer Motion), so the repo tells two different stories depending on where you look.
  • Rebranding a template is not the same as building on it. Stripping out the template's default e-commerce widgets early would have forced the real views to get built.

title: Happy Hour In My City
summary: A restaurant happy-hour discovery site to browse deals by city and neighbourhood on a map, with a dashboard where restaurant owners see their own listing.
html:
Overview

Happy Hour In My City (happyhourinmycity.com) is a restaurant happy-hour discovery site: browse and filter deals by city, neighbourhood and location on a map, with a directory of participating businesses. It's a Next.js app with a live public product for diners and a growing management layer for restaurant owners, starting with an owner dashboard backed by Supabase.

Problem

Happy hour deals are scattered across individual restaurant sites and social posts. There's no single place to discover what's on, where, and when, filtered by location. The goal was a directory-and-map product where a diner could find nearby deals at a glance, and where a restaurant owner could manage their own listing, including their own custom happy hours, instead of relying on someone else to keep it current.

What I built

  • A public discovery experience: home page with hero, listings, and a map section, plus /about, /mission, /faq (split into user and business FAQs), /join-restaurant, and /recommend for growing the directory
  • City and neighbourhood filters on the listings, so diners can narrow deals to the part of town they're actually in
  • Auth and account flows (/login, /signup) backed by Supabase, with role-gating middleware that checks a profiles table (role, approval_status, business_id) to protect /owner/* and /admin/* routes
  • An owner signup path that goes through /owner/pending-approval until an owner is approved, then into /owner/dashboard
  • A restaurant owner dashboard that resolves the signed-in owner's business_id from Supabase and shows that restaurant's offers and recurring happy-hour rules
  • An Airtable-backed content API (/businesses) pulling Businesses/Offers/Recurring Rules tables, with a local mock-data fallback so the app still runs without Airtable credentials in dev
  • Map display via @vis.gl/react-google-maps, with geocoding routed through the free Nominatim API instead of paid Google Geocoding to control cost
  • Legal/support pages (/disclaimer, /privacy, /terms), an offline PWA fallback page, and Capacitor scaffolding for a future native app wrapper
  • PostHog and Vercel Analytics wired in for usage tracking

Architecture

Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) with Tailwind v4 and shadcn/radix-ui components. Supabase handles auth and session state (@supabase/ssr), and middleware gates owner and admin routes based on the profiles table. Listing content (businesses, offers, recurring happy-hour rules) currently lives in Airtable: the /businesses route fetches it through Airtable's REST API, and the owner dashboard's /api/owner/restaurant route reads the owner's Supabase session, looks up their business_id, and pulls that business's records from Airtable. Map rendering uses the Google Maps JS API, while geocoding (converting addresses to coordinates) deliberately goes through free Nominatim rather than Google's paid geocoding endpoint. The admin dashboard is still a placeholder page.

Decisions

  • Moving listing content from Airtable to Supabase: Airtable was the right tool to launch with. The team could enter businesses, offers and recurring rules in a spreadsheet-like editor without building an admin UI first. It stops fitting once restaurant owners manage their own listings. Owners need to add custom happy hours (their own days, times and deals) and edit them from the dashboard, which means per-owner write access, validation and row-level permissions that Airtable isn't built for. Supabase already holds auth and owner profiles, so moving listings there puts the content and the people allowed to change it in one Postgres database, with row-level security tying each owner to their own business. It also drops the extra Airtable round-trip and its rate limits from every page load.
  • Nominatim over paid Google Geocoding: a deliberate cost-avoidance choice: the Google Maps key is scoped to JS map display only, keeping the app's per-request cost down while it's pre-revenue.
  • Building the role-gating middleware before the dashboards it protects: set up the access-control contract (who can see /owner/* and /admin/*) ahead of time, so the owner dashboard could be built directly against a working permission system rather than retrofitting auth later.

Results

A live public site with discovery, city and neighbourhood filtering, a business directory and account flows, promoted through happyhourinmycity.com, its register. subdomain, and Instagram/TikTok (@happyhourinmycity). Approved restaurant owners can sign in and see their own listing, offers and happy-hour rules in the owner dashboard.

What I learned

  • Pick a data store for who has to write to it, not just who reads it. Airtable was ideal while only the team edited content. Once restaurant owners needed to create their own custom happy hours, the store needed per-user permissions and validation, and that is what pushed the move to Supabase.
  • Building the permission layer first paid off. The owner dashboard went straight on top of the existing role and approval gating, with no auth retrofit.
  • An approval step between signup and dashboard keeps unvetted accounts away from listing data, which matters once owners can change what diners see.
  • Scoping paid APIs carefully (Google Maps for display only, free Nominatim for geocoding) matters for a pre-revenue local-discovery product, where per-request cost adds up fast as traffic grows.
  • A mock-data fallback for the content API made local development and onboarding easy, since nobody needed Airtable credentials just to run the app.

What's next

  • Migrate Businesses, Offers and Recurring Rules from Airtable into Supabase tables
  • Let owners create and edit custom happy hours from the dashboard, with row-level security limiting each owner to their own business
  • Build out the admin dashboard for owner approvals and listing moderation

title: NSE Stock Tracker
summary: A Streamlit app for exploring NSE (Indian exchange) stocks live: pricing, financials, and news pulled through the Yahoo Finance API.
html:
Overview

An interactive stock market tracker for NSE (National Stock Exchange, India) stocks, built with Streamlit and the Yahoo Finance API (yfinance). Co-built with Mark Allen while in grade XII at Arsha Vidya Mandir. It's one of the earliest real projects I shipped.

Problem

Understanding a stock's full picture (price history, financials, holders, analyst opinion, news) usually means jumping between several different tools and sites. The goal was one interface where picking a ticker gives access to all of that in one place, built to be understandable by people who aren't already market experts.

What I built

  • A ticker selector pulling the live NSE F&O stock list, feeding ~17 selectable features: stock summary, general info, historical data, price/volume plots, a calculator, major holders, balance sheet, cash flow, earnings, financials, actions, sustainability, analyst recommendations, earnings calendar, and latest news
  • Interactive price/volume charts (Plotly) with a configurable timeframe (from 1-minute to 3-month periods)
  • CSV export of any pulled dataset
  • A basic username/password login and sign-up module (SQLite-backed) gating access to the sidebar
  • A HTML-embedded navbar linking out to a companion YouTube playlist teaching stock market basics, aimed at the same beginner audience

Architecture

A single Streamlit app (Stock_Market_Tracker_Original.py) drives the whole experience: a sidebar ticker selector and feature selector, both backed by live calls to yfinance.Ticker(...). Selected data is rendered through pandas/Plotly directly in the page. A separate About.py Streamlit page carries the project's own writeup. A SQLite database (acc.db, via sqlite3) backs a simple userdetails table (username/password) for login and sign-up, checked against st.sidebar.button("Login") / st.sidebar.button("Sign Up").

Decisions

  • AlphaVantage → Yahoo Finance for data: AlphaVantage's free tier gated most of the interesting data behind a paywall; Yahoo Finance was free and unrestricted, so we switched early once that became clear.
  • Tkinter → Streamlit for the UI: Tkinter's learning curve and verbosity for even simple widgets made it a poor fit for two beginners; Streamlit replaced it (and absorbed what Matplotlib/pandas were doing for visualization) with far less code and a much shorter path to a working UI.

Results

A working Streamlit app covering the full range of stock research features listed above, live against real NSE market data.

What I learned

  • Picking the right tool early (Streamlit over Tkinter, Yahoo Finance over AlphaVantage) mattered more than pushing through with the first choice. Both pivots came from hitting a real wall, not from over-planning upfront.
  • This was an early lesson in scoping: a "track everything about a stock" feature list is easy to say and a lot of surface area to actually build.
  • Free data APIs come with trade-offs. yfinance was free and broad, but as an unofficial wrapper it can change or break without notice, so the app is only as reliable as its data source.
  • Building for beginners shaped what we built. The linked YouTube playlist on market basics exists because the audience was people new to investing, not market experts.

title: Onyx
summary: An ordering agent that buys from the suppliers a business already uses, with no supplier integration. It prices carts across stores by delivered cost and places approved orders through Agnic's Checkout Engine. Built for Agentic Commerce Pioneers Edition II.
html:
Overview

A solo build for Agentic Commerce Pioneers Edition II, Track 1 (Agentic Checkout). Onyx is an ordering agent for the suppliers a small business already buys from. A manager describes a restock in plain language with a budget. Onyx prices it against each supplier's real store, assembles the cheapest basket that covers the request and fits the budget, and places one order per supplier after a single approval. No supplier has to integrate.

Problem

A cafe orders the same things every week from several small suppliers. Each supplier has its own website, login, checkout and delivery charge. Comparing delivered cost across three carts by hand is tedious enough that nobody does it, so the business overpays. Most of these suppliers are small Shopify stores that will never build an API or an agent integration. Onyx is designed to work with them as they are.

What I built

  • Supplier onboarding from a URL. Onyx calls Agnic POST /explore, which drives the store's live checkout read-only and stops before payment. Onyx then stores the merchant id, rail, currency and discovered catalogue. Explore runs asynchronously for about two minutes, so Onyx tracks it with its own state machine.
  • Natural-language requests. An LLM parses the request into strict JSON, and Zod validates it before it becomes a Request row. The LLM provider is swappable.
  • Per-supplier live quotes. Onyx calls POST /shopify/quote with max_total_minor and max_shipping_minor caps on every call.
  • Delivered-cost basket assembly. An exact-cover search finds the cheapest non-overlapping set of supplier carts that covers every requested item within one budget, with a greedy fallback.
  • Approval and dispatch. Each supplier cart gets an immutable approval row with the exact items, destination and caps. Onyx then dispatches through POST /dispatch and polls GET /orders/{id} until the order reaches a terminal state and returns evidence.

Architecture

Next.js App Router frontend and API routes, Prisma on Neon Postgres, deployed on Vercel. The flow runs through five pages: /suppliers, /request, /price, /approve and /dispatch. Long operations never hold a request open. Explore and dispatch both persist state first and let the browser poll a short-lived route. If a serverless function dies mid-flight, the in-flight order is not lost.

Spending authority comes from a passkey-signed CAD mandate with per-purchase and daily limits, against a vaulted card that Onyx never sees. A purchase has to pass three separate checks before the card is touched: the API token's limits, the signed mandate, and the per-order caps recorded at approval.

Decisions

  • Assign items by delivered cost, not unit price. Each supplier ships separately, so a cheaper item can still lose once its own shipping is added.
  • Treat quotes with checkout-time tax as ceilings. Onyx labels them as ceilings and never compares them directly with a settled total.
  • Safety rules live in code, not just error handling:
    • Nothing is dispatched without an approval, and the approved payload is sent verbatim.
    • A conditional approved → dispatching update claims each order atomically, so it can't be charged twice.
    • The order id is saved before anything else. A timeout counts as an uncertain purchase and is polled, never retried blindly.
    • retryable: null halts everything and flags the order for a human.
  • Refusals are expected outcomes. A cap breach, an undeliverable destination or an unmatched item shows up as a labelled skip, not an error. Each supplier's order is independent, so one failure doesn't affect the others.

Results

Onyx attempted to onboard six real Canadian suppliers with no integration on their side. Five onboarded: Pilot Coffee Roasters, Bulkmart, Kim Eco-Pak, A1 Cash & Carry and Eight Ounce Coffee, all on Shopify. The sixth, Swish, was refused because its catalogue sits behind a trade account. In that case the engine stopped instead of guessing its way into a checkout it couldn't complete.

Onboarding, search, live quotes with real shipping, cap enforcement, the signed mandate and the full dispatch path all ran for real. Only settlement was simulated: purchases went through a sandbox store with a test card. One dispatch came back with retryable: null, and Onyx stopped as designed instead of retrying or refunding.

What I learned

  • In agentic checkout, the hard part is what happens when a purchase might or might not have gone through. Persisting state before acting, and refusing to blind-retry, matter more than the happy path.
  • A failure that stops cleanly is a stronger demo than one that's hidden. The retryable: null dispatch and the Swish refusal both showed the safety rules working on real stores.
  • Money-moving agents need layered limits. Token limits, a signed mandate and per-order caps each catch different mistakes, so no single bug or bad parse can overspend.
  • Optimize for what the customer actually pays. Comparing delivered cost instead of unit price can change which supplier wins an item, because separate shipping per supplier can wipe out a cheaper sticker price.
  • Serverless platforms punish long-held requests. Persisting state first and letting the browser poll short-lived routes made two-minute explores and slow dispatches survive function timeouts.

title: Route Optimizer
summary: A real-time route optimization app with a live traffic map, an AI chat assistant, and Solace-powered live messaging, built for Uottahacks7.
html:
Overview

A route optimization app built at Uottahacks7: a live map interface showing routes and traffic markers, an LLM-backed recommendation engine (Groq) that reasons about a route's traffic conditions, and a Solace PubSub+ connection that keeps the client aware of its real-time connection status for live updates.

Problem

Standard route-planning UIs show a route but not why it's a good one, and they don't adapt cleanly to live traffic conditions changing mid-trip. The goal was a route optimizer that treats traffic as a live signal driving the route, not a one-time input, and gives the user a conversational way to ask about it.

What I built

  • An interactive map (Leaflet) rendering routes and live traffic markers (Map.tsx, RouteMarkers.tsx, TrafficMarker.tsx)
  • A route panel presenting the optimized path and its details (RoutePanel.tsx)
  • An embedded chatbot widget for conversational trip assistance (ChatBotWidget.css, chatbot edge function)
  • A useSolaceConnection hook (SolaceConnection.tsx) that manages the Solace PubSub+ connection lifecycle client-side and surfaces connect/error state via toast notifications, backed by a get-solace-config edge function that hands the client its connection config
  • A Supabase edge function (optimize-route) that sends the current route and traffic data to Groq's mixtral-8x7b-32768 model and returns structured recommendations (alternative routes, expected delay severity, weather impact), with a safe default response if the Groq call fails

Architecture

React (Vite + TypeScript) frontend, styled with Tailwind and shadcn-ui, rendering the map via Leaflet. Three Supabase edge functions provide the backend: optimize-route builds a prompt from the route/traffic payload and calls the Groq chat completions API for recommendations, get-solace-config hands the client its Solace connection config, and chatbot serves the AI assistant. On the client, useSolaceConnection establishes and monitors the Solace connection so the UI can reflect real-time connectivity state.

Decisions

  • Supabase Edge Functions over a standalone backend: kept the whole stack deployable from one place under hackathon time pressure, without standing up separate backend infrastructure.
  • An LLM (Groq) for route recommendations instead of a hand-written optimization algorithm: turns route/traffic data into natural-language-derived recommendations (alternatives, delay severity, weather impact) without building a routing/optimization engine from scratch, at the cost of recommendations being only as reliable as the model's parsing of its own prompt response.
  • A safe fallback response when the Groq call fails or times out: the edge function always returns a 200 with a default recommendation rather than surfacing an error to the user, prioritizing a working demo over surfacing failures.

Results

Shipped as a working demo for Uottahacks7 combining live map routing, an LLM-driven recommendation engine, and Solace-backed real-time connectivity in one app.

What I learned

  • Prompting an LLM for structured output (route alternatives, delay severity, weather impact) and then parsing that back out of free text is fragile. The edge function's fallback logic exists because that parsing can't be fully trusted; asking the model for strict JSON and validating it against a schema would be the sturdier approach.
  • A silent fallback keeps a demo alive but hides failures. When the Groq call fails, the user gets a generic recommendation with no sign anything went wrong. Returning the fallback with a flag the UI can show would keep the demo working and stay honest.
  • Wiring a pub/sub layer (Solace) into a frontend app was new territory compared to typical request/response APIs. The UI had to react to connection-state changes (connecting, connected, dropped) rather than just waiting on fetch results.
  • Serverless edge functions are a fast way to stand up a backend at a hackathon: three small functions covered route recommendations, the chatbot and Solace config, with no server to deploy or keep running.

title: International Tax Administration Complexity Dashboard
summary: A Power BI dashboard ranking tax administration burden across economies, built on a custom weighted score derived from World Bank Doing Business indicators.
html:
Overview

A data analytics project comparing tax compliance burden across international economies, built entirely on public World Bank Doing Business "Paying Taxes" data. Python and pandas clean, merge, and score the raw indicators; Power BI turns the result into a comparative, rankable dashboard.

Problem

Tax compliance burden varies a lot by jurisdiction. Some economies demand more filing time, more separate payments per year, or a higher total tax rate, but there was no single transparent, reproducible score that combined those three signals into one ranking. The project answers: which economies in the dataset appear to have the most complex tax administration burden, based on public World Bank indicators?

What I built

  • A cleaning pipeline (merge_and_clean.py) that pulls three separate World Bank CSVs (PAY.TAX.TM, PAY.TAX.PYMT.FREQ.NO, PAY.TAX.TOT.TAX.RT.ZS), extracts the 2019 column from each, and merges them into one analytical dataset
  • Min-max normalization of each indicator into comparable 0 to 100 sub-scores (time_score, payments_score, tax_rate_score) in scoring.py
  • A weighted composite Tax Complexity Score: 0.40 * time_score + 0.30 * payments_score + 0.30 * tax_rate_score
  • Classification of economies into complexity bands based on that score
  • A Power BI dashboard for ranking, comparison, and stakeholder-facing visualization

Architecture

Three raw World Bank CSVs → merge_and_clean.py (pandas: select the 2019 column from each, inner-join on country, coerce numeric types, drop missing rows) → data/processed/tax_complexity_dashboard_ready.csv → scoring.py (min-max normalization + weighted composite score + banding into Low/Medium/High/Very High) → the processed CSV feeds a Power BI .pbix dashboard for the final visual layer.

Decisions

  • A transparent weighted formula over a black-box model: the 40/30/30 weighting is visible and adjustable, which matters for a dashboard meant to be defensible to stakeholders, not just accurate.
  • Min-max normalization per indicator before combining: the three raw indicators are on incompatible scales (hours, count, percent), so each is rescaled to 0 to 100 before the composite score is computed, keeping any one indicator from dominating by scale alone.

Results

Produces a ranked, banded comparison of tax administration complexity across every economy with complete 2019 data on all three indicators, visualized in an interactive Power BI dashboard (see images/dashboard_preview.png in the repo). In the processed output, Venezuela ranks highest at a complexity score of 63.5 ("High" band, driven by a 100/100 payments-frequency score); no economy in the dataset reaches the "Very High" band (75+).

What I learned

  • A single composite score is only as trustworthy as its weighting is explainable. Keeping the formula simple and visible mattered more than squeezing out marginal accuracy.
  • Working from three independently-sourced World Bank CSVs surfaced real messiness (missing years, inconsistent coverage) that a clean single dataset wouldn't have. The pipeline settles on a single fixed year (2019) across all three rather than each indicator's own latest year, which keeps the comparison apples-to-apples but means the dashboard isn't automatically current.
  • Joins quietly shape the result. The inner join drops any economy missing one of the three indicators, so the ranking only covers economies with complete 2019 data, and that limit has to be stated next to the ranking.
  • Normalization choices change rankings. Min-max scaling makes every score relative to the extremes in the dataset, so one outlier on payments frequency can compress everyone else's score.
